newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean defence minister removed in submarine row.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean defence minister removed in submarine row.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Thursday removed defence minister Lee Yang-ho after fierce criticism of the military for failing to intercept an intruding North Korean submarine.
Lee's departure was part of a sweeping reshuffle of the military top brass.
"This aims to renew the military atmosphere and to reinforce national defence by tightening military discipline," presidential spokesman Yoon Yeo-joon said, referring to Lee's removal.
The spokesman did not refer directly to the submarine incursion last month, which exposed gaping security holes and sparked calls for punishment for military officials.
South Koreans were shocked by the ease with which the Shark-class submarine penetrated South Korean coastal defences without triggering any alarm.

It was particularly worrying since South Korean military planning assumes any attack by North Korea on the South would be preceded by incursions by midget submarines landing saboteurs to blow up key facilities.
Some South Korean beaches are raked each day so that footprints of any infiltrators will show up.
Lee will be replaced by the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Kim Dong-jin, 58, a scholarly general who holds a masters degree in linguistics from Georgetown University in the United States.
Kim will be succeeded by the army chief of staff Yoon Young-nam.
Also being shifted are the commanders of all three South Korean armies and the deputy commander-in-chief of combined U.S.-South Korean forces.
Lee's departure was unscheduled, but the military commanders were all at the end of their terms.
"It is normal procedure for the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff to succeed the defence minister's position," the presidential spokesman said.
The submarine hit rocks off an east coast beach on September 18 and set ashore 26 North Koreans who fled to the mountains where 22 have been killed and one captured. Three are still missing.
Pyongyang has threatened "merciless retaliation" over the killings and demanded the return of the bodies, the survivors and the submarine.

On Tuesday, the U.N. Security Council issued a statement expressing "serious concern" over the incident and calling for strict observance of an armistice that ended hostilities in the 1950-53 Korean War.
Lee served as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff before joining the cabinet in 1994.
All the new appointments will take effect on Friday.
The cabinet change followed a meeting between Kim Young-sam and Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung on Thursday, Yonhap news agency reported.

The new army chief of staff will be Do Il-kyu, currently commander of the Third Army responsible for front-line defence against North Korea in the northwest sector of the country, which also embraces the capital, Seoul.
Commanders of the First and Second armies will retire and have not been named to new jobs.
The First Army covers the northeast part of the country, including the area where the submarine landed.

The deputy commander of combined U.S.-South Korean forces, Chang Sung, will be replaced by Kim Dong-shin. The commander of those forces is U.S. General John Tilelli, who also commands the 37,000 U.S. forces stationed in South Korea.
